syrupusdc-maple.text: Maple Finance's syrupUSDC has quietly become one of the largest yield-bearing stablecoins at $2.6 billion in deposits, all channeled into overcollateralized institutional loans returning 5-9% APY. The ERC-4626 vault design makes it composable enough that Aave V3, Morpho, and Pendle have all integrated it — meaning your lending yield can itself be lent, borrowed against, or split into principal and yield tranches. Base expansion in January 2026 saw a $50 million deposit cap fill immediately. The risk is the one that always haunts institutional credit: borrowers default, and "overcollateralized" is only as good as the collateral's liquidation value in a downturn.

syrupusdt-maple.title: The Mirror Vault
syrupusdt-maple.text: Maple's USDT counterpart to syrupUSDC runs on identical mechanics — ERC-4626 vault, institutional borrower pool, overcollateralized credit lines — but with $1.1 billion in deposits, it's the smaller sibling. The distinction matters less than it appears: both feed from the same Maple lending infrastructure, and yield differentials between the two are negligible. Ethereum-only deployment (no Base or Arbitrum yet) limits its DeFi composability compared to syrupUSDC, which may explain the size gap. For yield-seekers who prefer their stablecoin exposure in Tether rather than Circle, syrupUSDT is the vault; the economics are otherwise indistinguishable.

yousd-yield-optimizer.title: Fifty Strategies, One Token
yousd-yield-optimizer.text: YO Protocol's yoUSD automates what DeFi power users do manually — rebalancing USDC across 50+ yield sources on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, and Unichain, ranked by risk scores with per-pool and per-protocol concentration caps. The result: 8.64% annualized returns since March 2025 with zero negative months, which is the kind of track record that looks miraculous until you remember it was built during a bull market. Backed by Paradigm, Haun Ventures, and Coinbase Ventures, the $28 million in deposits is modest but growing. The real tension is philosophical: yoUSD is a sophisticated yield aggregator wearing a stablecoin's clothing, and its NAV appreciation model means your "dollar" is worth $1.07 and climbing — stable in the sense that it never goes down, not that it stays at one.

ustb-superstate.title: T-Bills Awaiting a Charter
ustb-superstate.text: Superstate's USTB is what happens when a fintech company decides the path to institutional credibility runs through the SEC's traditional fund registration process. At ~$876 million it is one of the larger tokenized T-bill products, trading at ~$11/share — a number that surprises anyone who expects a stablecoin dashboard entry to hold at $1. BNY Mellon holds the segregated account, Ernst & Young signs off annually, and sub-advisor Federated Hermes manages the actual T-bills while Superstate handles the on-chain tokenization. A pending conversion to a Section 2(a)(7) registered money market fund would make it the first on-chain MMF with that designation, unlocking institutional mandates currently blocked by fund policy. USTB's real market position is as yield-bearing infrastructure: it appears in the collateral stacks of frxUSD, m^0, and other stablecoins that want T-bill exposure without managing the compliance themselves.

ousg-ondo-finance.title: The Hundred-Dollar Stablecoin
ousg-ondo-finance.text: OUSG entered the market as a tokenized T-bill fund and quietly became BlackRock's largest single on-chain client — Ondo I LP migrated $95 million into BUIDL in March 2024 and has held that position since, making OUSG essentially a first-class derivative of BlackRock's tokenized money market presence. At roughly $113 per token, it is the least dollar-like entry on any stablecoin dashboard, which is why Ondo maintains rOUSG — a rebasing sibling that stays at $1 while OUSG appreciates. The November 2025 closure of an SEC investigation without charges removed the key regulatory overhang that had been suppressing institutional inflows. Restricted to U.S. Qualified Purchasers with on-chain KYC enforcement — tokens literally cannot transfer to non-whitelisted addresses — OUSG is less a stablecoin and more a tokenized mutual fund that borrowed the infrastructure.

cg-uscc.title: The Basis Trade, Institutionalized
cg-uscc.text: Calling USCC an RWA fund is technically accurate and culturally misleading — roughly half the portfolio consists of crypto cash-and-carry trades running long BTC, ETH, SOL, and XRP spot against short futures, with T-bills and Superstate's own USTB providing the buffer. The structure targets T-bill-plus returns without directional crypto exposure, a delta-neutral thesis compelling enough that Aave V3 absorbed $123 million of it as collateral and Sky (MakerDAO) allocated another $100 million. Whether the basis trade delivers consistent premium over T-bills depends on futures markets staying in contango — which tends to be true in bull markets and suspiciously fragile when it matters most. USCC is Superstate's more interesting product: less obvious than a T-bill fund, and less obvious about what its risk profile actually looks like during a crypto deleveraging event.

mtbill-midas.title: Europe's T-Bill Token
mtbill-midas.text: mTBILL is Midas's compliance-first answer to the tokenized T-bill race: a BlackRock IB01 ETF wrapper issued as a Liechtenstein FMA-approved MiFID II instrument, which is exactly the bureaucratic sentence required to legally sell T-bill exposure to European professionals. Ankura Trust provides daily on-chain NAV attestations, custody sits at Maerki Baumann in Switzerland, and the token contract is identical on Ethereum and Base — convenient deployment, if mildly unusual. The 'not available to U.S. or UK retail persons' restriction is the mirror image of USTB and OUSG's American access gates, carving out a European institutional niche in a market dominated by U.S. issuers. At $47 million mTBILL is the infrastructure layer in Midas's product stack — mF-ONE's liquidity sleeve depends on it, and it functions as stable collateral in third-party structured products.

wsrusd-reservoir.title: Ashes to APY
wsrusd-reservoir.text: Reservoir's rUSD processed $285M in redemptions 'without failure' in November 2025, then flatlined below $700K — the protocol's precise way of surviving a bank run while losing the patient. The protocol reincarnated as wsrUSD, an ERC-4626 NAV vault now at ~$96M, backing its stablecoin with an unusually varied diet: T-bills for bear-market floors, overcollateralized Morpho and Euler lending for DeFi rates, and crypto funding-rate strategies to capture bull-market upside. That flexibility is genuine; consistently beating benchmark yields through conditions that crushed simpler peers is not nothing. The catch is the governance label: allocations are voted by token holders, executed via multisig, and managed by named curators like Steakhouse and Gauntlet — all defensible arrangements, just a different thing from the 'permissionless and decentralized' framing that opens every piece of Reservoir marketing.

dusd-alto.title: The Isolated Vault Stablecoin
dusd-alto.text: Alto DUSD takes a kitchen-sink approach to collateral: mint markets accept WETH, three flavors of ETH LST, sUSDe, and Syrup USDC, while borrow markets add cbBTC, WBTC, tBTC, and PAXG into the mix — all in isolated markets so one bad collateral doesn't cascade into the rest. The PSM lets anyone swap DUSD for USDC at 20 bps, capped at 5M USDC, which is the primary peg anchor for a protocol whose total circulating supply barely clears $500K. Carrying sUSDe as accepted collateral creates an embedded Ethena dependency, meaning DUSD inherits a slice of delta-neutral basis risk on top of its overcollateralization buffer. ALTO token holders govern risk parameters, which is either reassuring decentralization or an early-stage DAO setting dials on a protocol nobody has stress-tested at scale.

dusd-dtrinity.title: The Borrower's Stablecoin
dusd-dtrinity.text: dUSD inverts the usual stablecoin economic model: instead of rewarding passive holders, it redirects float revenue from its USDC/USDT/sUSDS reserve to subsidize borrowers who take dUSD loans through dLEND, its Aave V3 fork. The mechanism is coherent — higher subsidized demand means higher utilization, which means higher yields for lenders, which attracts more reserves, which funds more subsidies — a flywheel that looks elegant at $2M circulating supply and unproven at any larger scale. Being backed entirely by other stablecoins creates a dependency stack: the peg inherits the counterparty risk of Circle, Tether, Sky, and Frax simultaneously, while the AMO and SMO add operational complexity that most comparably sized protocols don't carry. Deployed across Ethereum, Fraxtal, Katana, and Sonic with chain-isolated reserves, dTRINITY has built a sophisticated protocol for a market that has not yet shown up.

thbill-theo.title: Wrapping the Wrappers
thbill-theo.text: Theo's thBILL is a tokenized T-bill product one layer removed from the underlying treasuries: it holds tULTRA, which wraps Standard Chartered Libeara's ULTRA fund, which in turn holds the actual U.S. T-bills managed by Wellington Management. That's three entities and two wrappers between your token and a government bond. The Panama-incorporated, non-regulated structure contrasts sharply with the S&P-rated OpenEden TBILL it competes against, though Standard Chartered's custody and Wellington's management provide institutional ballast. At $132M AUM and growing fast, thBILL has found its niche among KYC'd investors who want T-bill exposure on HyperEVM, Base, and Arbitrum without caring too much about the wrapper depth.

usdp-parallel.title: Fee Yield, No Tricks
usdp-parallel.text: Parallel's USDp is a relatively small but architecturally interesting CDP: an overcollateralized basket of yield-bearing stablecoins (sfrxUSD, sUSDe) whose Parallelizer module adjusts minting and redemption fees dynamically to correct peg drift without oracles or liquidation cascades. The yield story is unusually honest — sUSDp distributes 70% of actual protocol fees from the Parallelizer, bridging, and flash loan modules, meaning yield tracks real usage rather than governance votes on a made-up rate. With a supply of roughly $3.5M since launching in September 2025, it's still early, but the Bailsec audit and Certora formal verification suggest Mimo Labs built this for durability rather than speed. The central tension is whether a fee-revenue yield model can remain attractive at $3.5M when it competes against synthetic dollar protocols running leveraged basis trades at hundred-fold the scale.

usdpt-western-union.title: Remittance Giant Meets Federal Charter
usdpt-western-union.text: Western Union moves $200B+ in cross-border remittances annually and has decided the next leg of that journey runs through Solana. USDPT is issued by Anchorage Digital Bank — the first federally chartered OCC crypto bank — with Western Union providing the distribution network spanning 200+ countries and half a million retail locations. The arrangement neatly sidesteps the "who regulates the issuer" question that haunts most stablecoin projects, since Anchorage already answers to the OCC. Whether a 170-year-old money transfer company can compete for on-chain liquidity against Circle and Tether remains the open question; the bet is that Western Union's physical footprint gives USDPT an on-ramp advantage nobody else can replicate.

roughrider-bnd.title: State-Owned Banking Goes On-Chain
roughrider-bnd.text: North Dakota's Bank of North Dakota — the only state-owned bank in the US — is building a wholesale stablecoin on Solana via Fiserv's infrastructure. Roughrider Coin is designed for bank-to-bank settlement, not consumer wallets, backed by USD reserves and 93-day Treasury notes. The pilot is pending ND Industrial Commission approval, making this one of the rare stablecoins whose launch date depends on a state government meeting agenda rather than a Discord vote. As the second US state stablecoin after Wyoming's FRNT, Roughrider represents an emerging pattern: state treasurers discovering that blockchain settlement is cheaper than correspondent banking, even if the branding choices remain firmly rooted in local pride.

fiusd-fiserv.title: The Payments Stack Play
fiusd-fiserv.text: Fiserv processes $2 trillion in payments annually for 6,000+ financial institutions and wants to make stablecoins just another rail in that plumbing. FIUSD is less a single stablecoin and more a platform: Paxos handles issuance, Circle provides ecosystem interop, PayPal enables interoperability, and Mastercard connects the payments network. The centralized-dependent classification captures this architecture accurately — FIUSD depends on an entire constellation of partners, any of which could become a bottleneck. The end-of-2025 launch target has quietly slipped into 2026 with no firm date, which either means careful regulatory preparation or the inherent difficulty of coordinating four major fintech companies on a shared timeline.

eur-qivalis.title: Twelve Banks, One Euro
eur-qivalis.text: Qivalis is the European banking establishment's answer to USDC and Tether: a MiCA-compliant euro stablecoin backed by a consortium of 12 major banks including BNP Paribas, ING, UniCredit, and BBVA. The reserve design — 40% bank deposits, 60% short-term eurozone government bonds — reads like a money market fund with a blockchain address. Qivalis B.V. is seeking an EMI license from the Dutch Central Bank, and no blockchain has been announced yet, which suggests the consortium is still negotiating whether they want Ethereum's liquidity or a permissioned chain's control. The central tension is whether twelve banks that compete fiercely in every other market can cooperate long enough to ship a product before Circle's EURC and SocGen's EURCV eat the entire MiCA-compliant euro stablecoin market.

pusd-polaris.title: Immutable CDP, Yield Included
pusd-polaris.text: Polaris Finance is building what its co-founders TokenBrice and 0xLuude call the successor to Liquity's ethos: a crypto-collateralized stablecoin on Ethereum with immutable core contracts, no admin keys, and no off-chain assets. pUSD is minted against pETH collateral via CDPs, and the yield-bearing angle comes from protocol revenue — borrowing interest, swap fees, conversion gains, and DEX fees — rather than from depositing reserves into Aave. The private testnet is live with a Q4 2026 target, which gives the team time to prove that you can ship immutability without sacrificing usability. For a market saturated with centralized fiat-backed tokens and yield products built on leverage, pUSD is a deliberate bet that there's still demand for the Liquity V1 philosophy, upgraded.

pgold-polaris.title: Synthetic Gold, No Vault Required
pgold-polaris.text: Polaris Gold shares infrastructure with its sibling pUSD but pegs to gold rather than the dollar — and critically, does so without any physical gold backing. Unlike XAUT or PAXG, which tokenize actual bars in Swiss vaults, pGOLD is a synthetic gold exposure minted from the same pETH collateral pool via CDPs on Ethereum. This makes it arguably more decentralized than any gold-pegged token on the market, at the cost of carrying all the risks of crypto collateral in a down market. Whether DeFi users want synthetic gold exposure from immutable contracts instead of custodied metal from Tether or Paxos is an experiment Polaris is willing to run.

usg-tangent.title: Productive Collateral, Dynamic Rates
usg-tangent.text: Tangent Finance is building USG as an over-collateralized CDP stablecoin that accepts productive DeFi collateral — Curve LP tokens, Pendle PTs, and Stake DAO positions — rather than raw ETH or stablecoins. The peg mechanism borrows from crvUSD’s playbook: instead of relying on redemptions, dynamic interest rates and a rewards deduction rate automatically increase when USG drifts below $1, incentivizing borrowers to repay. A yield-bearing sUSG vault (ERC-4626) lets holders capture protocol earnings passively, while TAN governance token holders direct the DAO and share revenue. The design bets that DeFi-native collateral can be more capital-efficient than traditional CDP models, though it inherits the composability risk of every protocol whose tokens it accepts.

klarnausd-klarna.title: Buy Now, Settle On-Chain Later
klarnausd-klarna.text: Klarna — the Swedish fintech with 114 million customers and $112B in annual GMV — is building a stablecoin via Stripe's Bridge infrastructure on the Tempo L1 (backed by a $500M Stripe/Paradigm raise). The initial use case is mundane by crypto standards but massive by payments standards: reducing Klarna's own cross-border settlement costs before expanding to consumer and merchant flows. Tempo testnet has been live since November 2025, though no official ticker has been disclosed. The interesting dynamic is that Klarna doesn't need external adoption for KlarnaUSD to succeed; its own payment volume is large enough to justify the infrastructure, making external DeFi liquidity a bonus rather than a requirement.

ussd-sonic-labs.title: Yield Without the Yield
ussd-sonic-labs.text: USSD is Sonic Labs' answer to why a fast EVM chain should depend on Circle and Tether to denominate everything — a permissionless, zero-fee stablecoin backed entirely by tokenized T-bills (BlackRock BUIDL, Superstate USTB, WisdomTree WTGXX) and built on Frax's frxUSD smart contract infrastructure. The design choice that distinguishes it from every other T-bill-backed stablecoin is also its most pointed: the Treasury yield flows to the Sonic ecosystem as buybacks and incentives, not to USSD holders, meaning every dollar sitting in USSD generates a return that benefits the protocol's treasury while the holder earns exactly $1. At roughly $2M in circulation at launch, this subsidy is trivial; at meaningful scale, it becomes a permanent off-balance-sheet revenue stream funded by users who chose the zero-yield option. The GENIUS Act-compatible framing and U.S. jurisdiction signal suggest Sonic Labs is building for a regulatory environment that hasn't fully arrived yet, which will look prescient or premature depending entirely on how fast Washington moves.
